Enjoy
en-JOY
v.
From Old French enjoir, to give joy to, from joie, joy. Webster 1828: to feel or perceive with pleasure; to take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession of. Scripture uses it of the pleasures of sin for a season, of God giving richly all things to enjoy, and of a land enjoying her sabbaths.

Biblical Definition

Enjoy in the Authorized Version is used with striking evenhandedness. Hebrews grants that sin has real pleasures and then weighs them: Moses chose rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season (Hebrews 11:25). The pleasures were genuine, the court of Egypt was genuinely comfortable, and the decisive word is season — Moses did arithmetic, having respect unto the recompence of the reward. Against that Paul commends enjoyment in the same letter where he warns the rich: Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). God is named as the giver, the giving is called rich, and the purpose is enjoyment — a sentence no ascetic reading of Scripture can absorb. Ecclesiastes says the same from the other end of a long experiment: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God (Ecclesiastes 2:24). And the word has a solemn use of the exile: then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34), the ground taking the rest Israel had refused to give it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ENJOY as to feel or perceive with pleasure; to take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of; and to possess with satisfaction. The possession and the pleasure in it are both included.

expand to see more

ENJOY, v.t. — To feel or perceive with pleasure; to take pleasure or satisfaction in the possession or experience of.

To possess with satisfaction; to occupy or have possession of, with pleasure; as, to enjoy health or an estate.

To have, possess and use with satisfaction; to have, hold or occupy, as a good or profitable thing.

ENJOYMENT, n. — The condition of enjoying; pleasure; satisfaction; fruition.

Webster’s insistence that enjoyment includes possession is useful: Leviticus 26:34 has the land enjoying sabbaths it was owed.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 11:25 — "Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;"

1 Timothy 6:17 — "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;"

Ecclesiastes 2:24 — "There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God."

Leviticus 26:34 — "Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths, as long as it lieth desolate, and ye be in your enemies’ land; even then shall the land rest, and enjoy her sabbaths."

Psalm 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Modern Corruption

Christianity is caricatured as the enemy of enjoyment, and too many Christians have earned the caricature; 1 Timothy 6:17 says God gives richly all things to enjoy, and the Westminster catechism makes enjoying Him man’s chief end.

expand to see more

The Shorter Catechism’s first answer is that man’s chief end is to glorify God and to enjoy him for ever, and the second verb is not decoration. Paul, warning the rich in the strongest terms against highmindedness and trust in uncertain riches, grounds the warning in a positive statement about God: He giveth us richly all things to enjoy. The remedy for the misuse of good things is not their renunciation but their right use with thanksgiving, which is exactly what the same apostle says against those forbidding meats: every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. Asceticism has an appearance of wisdom, Colossians says, and no value against the indulgence of the flesh.

Hebrews 11:25 keeps the other rail in place, and it does so without pretending. Sin has pleasures. Scripture never argues that wickedness is unpleasant, which is a lie any honest person can detect, and the moment a preacher tries it he loses the young people who know better. The argument is about duration and about what is being traded: for a season, against the recompence of the reward. Moses was doing sums, not suppressing appetite. Psalm 16:11 states the alternative offer in full — fulness of joy and pleasures for evermore — and no season of Egypt’s pleasures competes with it once the terms are seen.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apolausis (G619), enjoyment, from apolauo, to have full benefit of; Hebrew ratsah (H7521), to be pleased with or to enjoy, of the land’s sabbaths.

expand to see more

Greek apolausis (G619) — enjoyment, fruition; 1 Timothy 6:17 and Hebrews 11:25, the only two occurrences.

Greek apolauo — to have full benefit of, to enjoy; the verb behind the noun.

Greek prokairos (G4340) — for a season, temporary; the pleasures of sin for a season.

Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to accept, to enjoy; the land shall enjoy her sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34).

Hebrew ra’ah tob — to see good, the idiom rendered enjoy good at Ecclesiastes 2:24.

Usage

"Than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season (Hebrews 11:25) — the pleasures granted, and their term stated."

"Who giveth us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17) — the ground of a warning to the rich."

"Then shall the land enjoy her sabbaths (Leviticus 26:34) — rest taken by the ground in exile."
